title: Khoresh gheymeh
subtitle: Persian split pea and lamb stew with saffron
excerpt: Khoresh gheymeh is a Persian yellow split pea and diced lamb stew with saffron and dried lime, finished with crispy fried potato sticks on top. It is one of the most popular khoresh in Iran and often served at gatherings and feasts alongside chelow.
sourceNotes: Najmieh Batmanglij, Food of Life: Ancient Persian and Modern Iranian Cooking and Ceremonies (1986). Khoresh gheymeh documented as one of the four classic khoresh, with notes on the dried lime technique. Margaret Shaida, The Legendary Cuisine of Persia (1992). Regional variations and the potato topping discussed.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the stew without the potato topping. Reheat gently and add fresh fried potatoes before serving.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well. Make a large batch and freeze in portions.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The stew improves if made a day ahead. Reheat slowly with a splash of water to loosen.

content.text: Khoresh gheymeh is a slow-cooked Persian stew of diced lamb and yellow split peas, deepened with saffron and the sharp, slightly bitter flavour of dried lime. Dried limes (limu omani) are not easy to find outside Middle Eastern shops; a combination of lime zest and juice gives a reasonable approximation. The stew is finished with a layer of fine potato matchsticks fried until crisp, which give texture contrast to the soft stew beneath.

items.prepNote: soaked in cold water for 1 hour, drained
ground, dissolved in 3 tbsp hot water
zest and juice (substitute for dried lime)
peeled and cut into fine matchsticks

content.text: Heat {{olive-oil}} in a wide heavy pot over a medium-high heat. Add {{onion}} and fry for fifteen minutes, stirring often, until deeply golden and caramelised.
Add {{turmeric-ground}} and stir for one minute. Add {{lamb-shoulder}} in batches, browning it well on all sides. Return all the lamb to the pot.
Add {{tinned-tomatoes}}, {{tomato-puree}}, {{cinnamon-ground}}, {{sea-salt-fine}}, {{black-pepper}}, lime zest and juice from {{lime}}, and 400 ml of water. Stir and bring to the boil.

Reduce to a low simmer. Add the soaked, drained {{split-peas-yellow}} and the dissolved {{saffron}}. Cover and simmer for 60 to 75 minutes until the lamb is very tender and the split peas are soft and beginning to break down. Stir occasionally and add a splash of water if needed.
Taste and adjust the seasoning. The stew should be thick, not soupy.

Heat {{sunflower-oil}} in a frying pan to 180 degrees. Pat the {{potato}} matchsticks dry with kitchen paper. Fry in two batches for two to three minutes each until golden and crisp. Drain on kitchen paper and season with salt.
Spoon the stew into a serving bowl and pile the crispy potato sticks on top. Serve with chelow.

items.symptom: The split peas are still hard after an hour
items.cause: Not soaked, or simmered at too low a heat
items.fix: Soaking for an hour is important. Cook at a steady, gentle simmer rather than a bare whisper. Add more time as needed.

items.cause: Too much water added or lid was off during cooking
items.fix: Simmer uncovered for the last fifteen minutes to reduce. The stew should be thick enough to mound on a spoon.

items.symptom: The lime flavour is too sharp
items.cause: Too much lime juice relative to other flavours
items.fix: Add the juice in two stages, tasting between additions. The lime should be noticeable but not dominant.

items.symptom: The potato matchsticks are soft, not crispy
items.cause: Oil not hot enough or too many potatoes added at once
items.fix: Heat the oil to 180 degrees before adding the potatoes. Fry in small batches so the temperature stays high.

content.text: Khoresh gheymeh is one of the most common dishes at Iranian celebrations, weddings, and gatherings, where large pots are cooked for hundreds of guests alongside chelow. The name gheymeh means small diced pieces of meat. The key ingredient in the authentic version is limu omani, the dried Persian lime. It gives a sour-bitter note that fresh citrus cannot match; lime zest and juice is a workable substitute. Most Iranian families now make the version with a crispy potato topping. Older recipes use fried aubergine slices instead.
